shortSummary: Mo Khazali uses automotive and factory-history analogies to argue that AI adoption needs a redesigned delivery system. Shared platforms, daily learning, early quality checks and customer-outcome measures matter more than token consumption or code output alone.
longSummary: Mo Khazali compares today's AI adoption with manufacturers investing in automation while leaving their working systems largely unchanged. Through the Detroit, NUMMI and factory-electrification stories, he argues for redesigning the flow of work rather than expecting better tools to repair an organisation by themselves. He applies ideas from the Toyota production system and the Lean Tech Manifesto to software: an AI platform team shares useful building blocks, teams practise daily problem-solving, reference blueprints and deterministic checks catch recurring defects, and the working week is adapted to the team's actual constraints. His examples emphasise learning from friction and feeding local improvements back into the wider organisation. He closes by shifting attention toward what to build and how to measure it: delivery flow, failures, recovery, rework and value for customers, rather than licences, token leaderboards or generated code volume.

takeaways.point: Tool adoption and activity measures do not by themselves demonstrate customer value or an improved delivery system.
An AI platform team can turn local solutions into shared model access, observability, skills, standards and support.
Daily experiments and root-cause discussions develop a learning culture beyond a one-off rollout or workshop.
Reference blueprints and deterministic rules can prevent known classes of mistakes and reduce repeated correction.
Audit the whole flow and track outcomes, failures, rework and customer value as bottlenecks shift toward deciding what to build.
